text: As for you, raise a lament over the princes of Israel.
Say: What a lioness was your mother! Among lions she lay down; among young lions she reared her cubs.

versions.text: Say: What a lioness was your mother among the lions! She lay down among the young lions and reared her cubs.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two parallel clauses: 'among lions she lay down' and 'among young lions she reared her cubs.' The current rendering attaches 'among the lions' to the opening exclamation and shifts 'young lions' into the first clause, blurring the parallelism. The restored parallel structure is also stronger for oral reading.

text: She raised up one of her cubs; he became a young lion. He learned to tear his prey; he devoured men.
The nations heard of him; he was caught in their pit, and they led him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
When she saw that her waiting was in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion.
He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion. He learned to tear his prey; he devoured men.

He broke down their strongholds and laid waste their cities; the land and all who filled it were appalled at the sound of his roaring. [^1]

[^1]: The Hebrew text here reads literally 'he knew his widows'; 'broke down their strongholds' follows a slight difference in the consonants supported by ancient versions.

versions.text: He broke down their strongholds and laid waste their cities; the land and all who filled it were appalled at the sound of his roaring.
versions.explanation: This is a well-known textual crux; a brief footnote alerts the reader that the rendering rests on a small emendation without disturbing the readable text.

text: Then the nations closed in on him from the provinces all around. They spread their net over him; he was caught in their pit.
With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon. They brought him into strongholds, so that his voice would never again be heard on the mountains of Israel.

versions.text: With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon. They put him in prison, so that his voice would never again be heard on the mountains of Israel.
versions.explanation: The verb is again 'they brought him,' and מְצֹדוֹת means 'strongholds/fortresses,' not 'prison.' The repetition of 'brought' is deliberate in the Hebrew and reads well aloud.

text:
Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches from the abundant water. [^1]

[^1]: 'In your blood' renders an obscure Hebrew phrase; it may mean 'in your vineyard' or 'in your likeness.'

versions.text: Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches from the abundant water.
versions.explanation: 'In your blood' is opaque to a listening audience; a short footnote explains the difficulty without altering the text.

text: Its branches grew strong, fit for the scepters of rulers. It towered high above the thick foliage, conspicuous in its height and in the mass of its boughs.
But it was uprooted in fury and thrown to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were broken off and withered; fire consumed them.
Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a land of drought and thirst.
Fire went out from the stem of its branches and consumed its fruit, so that no strong branch was left in it, no scepter for ruling. This is a lament, and a lament it shall remain.

versions.text: Fire went out from its stem and consumed its shoots and its fruit, so that no strong branch was left in it, no scepter for ruling. This is a lament, and a lament it shall remain.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew, 'its branches' belongs to the phrase 'from the stem of its branches'; the only object of 'consumed' is 'its fruit.' The current wording turns the shoots into an additional object, adding content not in the text.
